1:
Gill and Clarke both number this the fourth vision, Clarke reading it as denoting the certainty and nearness of the ruin. Keil and Delitzsch sets out the whole chapter from it: the basket shows that Israel is ripe for judgment, whereupon Amos announces to the unrighteous magnates the changing of their feasts into days of mourning, and then sets before them a time when men who now despise the word of God will sigh in vain for a word from him. Henry begins further back. The great reason sinners defer repentance is that they suppose God defers his judgments, and there is no song with which they so effectually sing themselves asleep as that their Lord delays his coming; so God represents the day of his wrath as not merely certain but near. Henry presses the question the vision asks, whether we do indeed see what God has shown us, since many a thing he speaks once and twice and men perceive it not; if we are in the midst of the visions of the Almighty, let us consider what we see. Gill gives the question the same purpose, to quicken a man who might pass the basket by as a common thing.

What the fruit meant is drawn out in several directions that agree. Henry takes it that they were ripe for destruction, rotten ripe, so that it was time to put in the sickle; that the year of God's patience was closing, autumn with them and a dismal winter next; and that summer fruits will not keep till winter but must be used at once, an emblem of a people with nothing solid in them. Clarke reasons from the keeping quality, that such fruit had to be eaten as gathered, so that punishment must descend without delay; and he reports another view, that the fruits meant are those of the end of autumn, after which none could be expected, so that Israel's summer is gone and she shall yield no more, or else that the autumn of her iniquity has come and the measure is filled. Calvin makes the ripeness belong to the punishment rather than the people, a ripe vengeance no longer to be deferred, and adds that the fruits intended have no solid vigour to last.

All notice the play of words. Calvin says the likeness between the Hebrew term for summer fruit and the term for an end cannot be reproduced in Greek or Latin, only one letter separating them; Clarke names it a paronomasia and points to a similar play in another prophet; Henry observes that the word signifying the end is of near affinity with the word for summer fruit.

Calvin explains what the long forbearance had been for. God had struck that people with a suspended hand and spared them even in their greatest calamities, alluring them by forbearance to repentance; but they had grown so refractory that such remedies no longer benefited them. Hence the meaning of not passing by them again, which Calvin refers to punishment: God chastises because he is solicitous for their salvation, and to pass by no more is to spend no further labour on men whom correction does not reach. He puts it as a challenge: their iniquity is ripe and they may gather the fruit, since they cannot proceed one day further. Wesley says the same of both ends at once, the end of God's patience and the end of their ripening, so that they are fit to be gathered, having been spared with admirable patience and now to be spared no longer; and Clarke reduces the clause to a phrase, that God will be no longer their guardian. Calvin notes on the opening formula that the prophet adduces nothing without authority but faithfully relates what was commanded from above, since God so employed his prophets as to reserve the right of teaching to himself.
3:
Where the songs were sung is disputed. Ellicott notes that the word rendered temple also means palace and thinks that the likelier sense here. Clarke reports a conjecture that changes one word so that the line reads the singing women of the palace shall howl in that day, and observes that instead of joyous songs they shall have nothing but lamentation. Calvin keeps the temple and makes the singing itself the offence. Unbelievers misconstrue both the hatred and the favour of God by the present appearance of things, looking not at themselves but at their circumstances, so that while God indulges them they never doubt he is on their side; he instances the men of Sodom, who thought they had peace with heaven to the hour of their destruction, and the feasting and building in the days of Noah. The particular vice here, he says, is that the people sang in their temples while the voices of the prophets resounded daily with grievous threatenings, as though they meant to mock God designedly; and so for melody the prophet names howling.

The clause about casting forth is harder still. Ellicott calls the construction doubtful and reports two attempts at it, one breaking the sentence into abrupt ejaculations and another reading the verb as an imperative on the authority of two manuscripts; he prefers, as more in keeping with the style of Amos, to connect the clauses so that there shall be many corpses in every place that one has cast away in hushed silence, which describes the reign of death with none to bury or lament. Clarke gets to the same picture another way, that every place shall be filled with the dead and a dreadful silence reign, the few who remain being afraid to speak or even to chant a dirge for the most respectable of the dead. Wesley reads the silence as the enemy's doing, whose cruelty is such that they dare not bury the dead, or if they do it must be undiscerned.

The address that follows is aimed at a class. Calvin observes that the prophet assails the princes by name, and explains why: the whole state was corrupt from highest to lowest and none was free from blame, but more guilt always belongs to leaders, since the common people go astray through thoughtlessness or are led on by others, while those who govern pervert what is just and become the originators of every licentiousness. He hears an emphasis in the command to hear, given either because such men did not observe their own sins and were wholly deaf, or because they contended with God in vain, hypocrites supposing evasion will carry them past judgment. Henry describes the same men by an older figure, the unjust judge who neither feared God nor regarded man, and notes the order of the two failures, since those who have lost the savour of piety will not long retain the sense of common honesty.

On the swallowing Gill supplies the image, a man who pants after water when thirsty and gulps it at once, which is how these rich men took in the poor, their labour and gains and persons too, until they held everything and had made bondsmen of them; and he adds why they of all people are summoned to hear it, since their oppression was itself one cause of the destruction announced. Ellicott would render the clause more sharply still, as panting for the very ashes on the heads of the poor, and gives the second verb its literal force, to make them cease, that is to destroy them.
5:
What the new moon was is variously explained. Gill takes it for the first day of every month, on which selling was forbidden because the day was appointed for religious service; and he reports two Jewish alternatives, that the word means the month of harvest, when the poor gleaned enough and had no need to buy, so that hoarders wished it over in order to sell again, or the month intercalated every three years to bring the feasts right with the season. Clarke calls the new moon a holy day kept by custom rather than by divine command, and grants the men one point, that bad as they were they did not actually set out their corn on the sabbath itself, though they grudged God that seventh portion of time. Ellicott draws a historical inference from the complaint, that these festivals must have been observed in the northern kingdom even if disliked, since the impatience is for their ending; and he takes the desire to be not merely for secular employment but for the pursuit of ill-gotten gain. Wesley says the men could wish nothing interrupted their marketing.

The frauds themselves are itemised. Ellicott explains the mechanism: the ephah was a dry measure of about three English pecks, made small so that less should be sold, while the shekel was the weight against which the metal was weighed and was augmented so that more silver was demanded for the impoverished measure; he would render the last clause as falsifying the deceitful balances, so that the symbol of justice became the implement of injustice. Clarke states the same in the seller's terms, short measure and full price, one end of the beam long and the other short. Wesley counts the loss twice, since with the measure too little the buyer had not his due, and with the weight too great he paid more than he owed. Ellicott glosses the phrase about setting forth wheat as the opening of the sacks or granaries where it was stored.

Calvin sets the whole against a background of scarcity. The charge cannot apply to the whole people, he says, but only to the plunderers who had abundance of corn and could oppress the poor; a few men in a time of want hold the provisions hoarded and so put miserable men to death by reducing them to need. Since the few held the whole people in famine, the prophet may fairly ask whether God deals rigidly. To the objection that the slaughter threatened earlier was to fall on everyone alike, he answers that other vices needed correction too, but a beginning had to be made with the proud, who relied on their dignity and thought themselves exempt from the common lot.

Buying the poor is read as debt-slavery. Gill has them made to pay dear until they cannot support their families and are then purchased with their households for a single coin; Clarke as buying their service for a term with just enough to clear them with other creditors; Wesley as taking advantage of a man who owed only for some trifle and making him sell himself to pay it. Calvin explains why such a trade works: men oppressed with famine will sooner sell their life a hundred times over than fail to rescue it at any price, since food is nothing but the support of life, and the rich watched for that moment. The refuse aggravates it. Calvin notes that having reduced the poor to bondage they did not even feed them properly, mingling offscourings with the wheat, selling barley for wheat and chaff for barley, and says this wrong is neither new nor unusual. Clarke has them selling damaged flour as good, knowing the poor cannot afford to prosecute; and Ellicott remarks that the money-making propensity ran to such lengths that they sold what was little better than chaff.
7:
Calvin explains why an oath is needed at all. Being merely reproved would not have troubled such men, who had grown shameless and hardened, and whose insatiable cupidity had so blinded them that they cast aside every care for what was right; though the whole people cried out against them and God thundered from heaven they laughed it all to scorn. So that the threatening might penetrate, the prophet puts it in the form of a divine oath. What God swears by is then disputed. Gill sets aside two Jewish suggestions, the ark and the temple, and takes the excellency of Jacob for God himself, the most excellent of all that Jacob possessed and the proper subject of his boasting. Wesley says simply, by himself. Clarke allows two senses, either the state of eminence to which God had raised that people, or the excellent One of Jacob, that is God, and paraphrases the oath accordingly: as surely as I raised you to such eminence, so surely will I punish you in proportion to your advantages and your crimes. Ellicott notices that the same phrase appeared earlier as something God abhorred, and reconciles the two: what he abhorred was the miserable substitute the people had made for his great Name, whereas here he gives the phrase the value it ought in itself to possess. Calvin rejects an older rendering that made it he has sworn against the pride of Jacob, on the ground that the prophet speaks not of a vice but of the dignity God had conferred on the posterity of Abraham, the very privilege on which they wrongly counted themselves safe.

The question that follows is read by Calvin as a double affirmation. A question is put, he says, where there is no room for doubt at all, and the sense is that men who had perverted everything right and just and were moved by no feeling of humanity could not possibly remain in safety. He presses the figure of the shaking land as a kind of personification: when such men mingle heaven and earth together, the land cannot stay quiet while it sustains inhabitants with whom it has no agreement, and so must necessarily be agitated. He notes that the current sense of the verb is to shake or move, and finds it the most suitable here. Wesley shifts the reference from the ground to the people, taking the land for its inhabitants, and reads the rising as the judgment growing like a mighty wasting flood.

Whether a literal earthquake is meant divides the voices. Gill thinks so, and points to the one that came two years after the prophet began, though he offers alternatives, that the earth might gape and swallow such men alive, or that the inhabitants would tremble at the judgments sworn against them. Clarke agrees that an earthquake is supposed, and explains the rising and subsiding as the heaving motion of one, compared here to the overflowing and falling of the Nile; but he leaves open that the words may refer instead to commotions among the people. Ellicott keeps the earthquake and sharpens the comparison, rendering the clause that the whole of it rises as the Nile and surges and subsides as the Egyptian Nile does, and noting that the river ascends some twenty feet in the time of its inundation before it sinks again. Wesley keeps the flood but makes the drowning the point, that the land shall be overwhelmed as Egypt is by the overflowing of its river. Calvin sets the sequence out in order: the earth, ceasing to fulfil its offices, constrains its inhabitants to lament and mourn, and then the second figure shows the moving of the earth, that it will rise like a river and destroy men with a deluge.
9:
Whether a real eclipse stands behind this verse is the sharpest disagreement in the chapter. Clarke offers two possibilities, the darkness that often precedes and accompanies earthquakes, or an eclipse, and reports a computation that about eleven years after the prophet spoke there were two great eclipses of the sun, one at the feast of tabernacles and the other shortly before the passover; yet on balance he thinks the whole passage refers to the earthquake. Gill goes much further and gives three of them with their dates and magnitudes, at pentecost, at tabernacles eleven years later, and at the passover in the year following, and says the prophecy may refer literally to these and to the alarm at what they were thought to forebode. Ellicott holds that an eclipse can hardly be doubted here, since the earthquake of the previous verse is used figuratively in just the same way, and reports at length a scholar's attempt to identify it with one recorded in the Assyrian annals and calculated to a day, remarking that if the prophet had that eclipse in mind the fact carries weight for chronology. Calvin denies the whole approach. It is certain, he says, that this was not the eclipse of the sun and that the prophet did not mean one; the expression is figurative, and a man disposed to lay hold on what is literal and cleave to it would have gross and insipid notions not only of the prophets but of every other writing, since no language is without its figures.

What the figure conveys the same voices agree on. Calvin puts the sense in the prophet's mouth: you congratulate yourselves on your wealth and on all that delights you, as though God could not turn light into darkness, and because he spares you you suppose it will always be so; but he can, and a dark night will overtake you at midday. Wesley reads it historically of a kingdom whose sun set at noon under conspiracies and civil wars, with the midnight coming on afterwards by the hand of named invaders, and glosses the last clause as darkness falling in the clear day, when men think all is safe and well settled. Ellicott takes the darkening of the sun at noon as an image of confusion and terror, standing for national calamity, the extinction of the royal house and perhaps the final overthrow of the kingdom.

The turning of feasts into mourning is read at two levels. Gill offers the literal one first, that the eclipses he has dated fell at the three great feasts, and then the fuller sense, that these feasts could no longer be observed at all nor their songs sung any more; or else that the feasting meant is the mirth and jollity of their own houses, now to be exchanged for lamentation. Clarke says only that a bitter day is a time of grievous calamity. Calvin explains why feasts and songs in particular are named. The people flattered themselves on their ceremonies while those very ceremonies provoked God the more, since the worship they professed was mere superstition and so a profanation of true religion; as another prophet says, ceremonies are to hypocrites the dens of robbers. So the threat is aimed exactly there: they thought their festivals were expiations that turned aside vengeance, when in truth they were the fans by which they kindled it. Wesley completes the picture of the mourning itself, that sackcloth on all loins means every sort of person put into mourning, that shaving the head and beard was the sign of the greatest sadness, and that the bitter day which succeeds the dark night is one they will wish they had never seen.
11:
Henry sets the threat against what the people then had. When Amos prophesied they enjoyed great plenty of prophets, precept upon precept, so that prophecy was their daily bread; and it is probable, he says, that they surfeited on it as their fathers had on the manna, which is why God threatens to take the privilege away. The famine itself he defines by contrast: not of bread and water but a much sorer judgment, in which there shall be no congregations for ministers to preach to nor ministers to preach, and men shall have the written word to read but nobody to explain and apply it, the water in the well and nothing to draw with. He notes that elsewhere it is a gracious promise that though bread be scarce the means of grace shall not be, and recalls the saying that brown bread and the gospel are good fare. Three things follow. It was the departure of much of the nation's glory, since what made them high was that to them were committed the oracles of God. It was a token of the highest displeasure, God speaking to them no more nor affording the means that might bring them to repentance. And it made every other calamity melancholy, since they had no prophets to comfort them.

Clarke calls it the most grievous of famines, a time when no prophet should appear and no faithful reprover, and reckons it the severest of God's judgments short of the fire that is never quenched. Gill reports one view referring it to the whole period after the last of the prophets, but prefers the carrying away of the ten tribes, when none was left to tell them how long their captivity should last. Calvin makes it heavier still, not temporal punishment but final destruction and an evidence of reprobation, God depriving them of every light of truth so that they wander like blind men in the dark. He grants they had long been bereaved of sound doctrine; but God had restrained them as it were against their will, goading them and trying by force to bring them back, and only when he saw his servants' labour wholly fruitless did he denounce a final vengeance.

Calvin then raises an objection against himself. If they are to hunger for the word, is that not itself a favour, since a desire for sound doctrine shows some religion remains, and since it is promised that those who seek shall find? He answers that the prophet does not mean they would sincerely seek it, but that they would learn by the punishment that nothing is more to be dreaded than the loss of the soul's food. His instance is Esau, who cried and howled when he saw his birthright gone, not from right feeling but urged by despair alone; so the reprobate, stripped of God's favours, are not moved to repent but only feel strong agonies and torment themselves without benefit.

The wandering is mapped differently by each. Gill offers the sea of Tiberias, or the Dead Sea, running to the great sea in the west. Clarke draws it from the Mediterranean to the Dead Sea, west to east and north to south, in search of any man authorised to show them the end of their calamities. Henry has them going from one border to another to see whether God will send prophets by sea or land out of other countries, since they have none at home. Wesley says they will search all corners for a prophet. Ellicott renders the verbs as staggering and reeling, to find one seer who knows the mind of the Lord and find none, and interprets the compass points: the east probably means Arabia and the tract beyond it, the north the country toward Aram, and it was from those districts that the people had sought vain help in idolatrous divination.
13:
What the thirst is divides Gill from Calvin. Gill continues the figure and reads it of the want of the word, and of the grain and wine that make young men and maids cheerful, so that being destitute they are overwhelmed with grief; he reports two further applications, that the virgins are the congregation itself and the young men its principal persons, or that both stand for men trusting to their own righteousness who never hungered after a better one. Calvin refuses to take the thirst in the sense used before, and understands a literal drying up through want of everything. A country may lack provisions while water is still to be had, he says, but when even that fails it is evidence of almost the extreme curse; so when God took away the word by which souls are nourished, the people would be left without bread and without water too. He notices what the mention of the young is for: it seems unnatural that the vigorous, who can run to supply their wants, should faint, and the point is that there would be no escape, since God distresses even the strongest. Ellicott presses the same inference the other way, that if fair virgins and strong youths faint for thirst the less vigorous must suffer more keenly still; and he turns it into a question about age, that it is sad when old men stumble into unbelief in the noon-day sun, since they at least remember the brightness of their morning and may hope for light at evening, but asks what becomes of the young who are veiled at the outset, and where the elders will be if they have had no youth.

The sin of Samaria is variously identified. Gill and Ellicott take it for the golden calf worshipped there, Gill adding that the making of it was the effect of sin and the occasion of sin, and that men swore by it as they had been used to swear by the living God, so setting an idol on a level with him. Clarke names Baal instead. Calvin reports and rejects a metaphorical reading in which sin means a sin-offering, a sense the word does bear elsewhere, calling it too refined; the prophet speaks of the idols themselves, called wickedness by way of reproach though their worshippers gave them the honourable name of a god. He explains the geography, that it is called the sin of Samaria because that was the royal residence and the chief city from which the corruption of the country flowed, the prophet naming the source and then instancing the two shrines. Ellicott records and sets aside a modern proposal that the phrase refers to a different cult altogether.

The last oath is the obscurest. Clarke takes the word rendered manner in its plain sense of way, used here for the object and mode of worship, and compares the New Testament use of the same term for a creed and form of worship; the thing sworn by he makes another of the golden calves. Ellicott renders the clause by the life of the way of Beersheba and takes the way for the ritual practised there, which is itself another mode of designating the deity; he adds that the place lay far south on the borders of the other kingdom, some distance below Hebron, and was so famous a religious centre that men of the north were in the habit of crossing the frontier to pay their vows there. Wesley says only that the manner means the idol worshipped at that place, and that those meant are the men who sacrifice to and swear by the calves.
